Discussion Eleven of the 14 sites sampled were con- sidered to have reliable mean-site remanence directions. The strike and dip of the diabase sheet at the 11 sites (Table I) were obtained from information compiled by Thomson ( 1960, pp. 18-20; 1961a, pp. 46-47; 1961b, pp. 17, 19, 22, 24, 52; 1961c, p. 43). All tectonic corrections were made by simple rotation of the dip plane to the horizontal about the strike. Applying the fold test (Graham 1949) to all 11 mean site remanence directions, the values of a95 before and after tectonic correction were 5.4' and 8.6" respectively. Snedecor's F-ratio test for the null hypothesis (Larochelle 1968) indicates that there is a probability of 0.97 that the scatter in the remanence directions caused by applying tectonic corrections is significant. These tests show that the diabase acquired its remanence after solidification of the primary basin and arch structure. There is some evidence that Thomson's (1957) suggestion that post-solidification tec- degrees. tonics accentuated the basin and arch structure is correct. The

post-solidification NW- SE contraction approximately perpendicular to the basin axis (N 50°E) and parallel to the major NW-SE fault set. Unfortunately 3 of the 4 sites (5, 6, 7, and 8) collected to define the limbs of the Kerr Lake Arch which might have provided useful additional data, are not reliable. Thus the data favor a minor amount of secondary folding but not on a statistical significance basis. Sites 9 and 10 are adjacent to the Beaver and Kerr Lake faults respectively where the diabase sheet dips at 60' and 15" respectively. Application of tectonic corrections causes the remanence directions to scatter from consistent primary directions to completely inconsistent directions. This result suggests that the diabase SYMONS: PAL was not folded by more than a very few de- grees adjacent to the major faults contrary to Knight's ( 1922) suggestion. Sites 11 to 14 are collected on a N-S traverse perpendicular to the E-W ore vein structures of the Silverfields mine where the diabase sheet is flat-lying (Moore 1967; Petruk 1968). If post-solidification tectonics caused the sheet to fracture into blocks defined by the veins, then the remanence directions might reflect some consistent deformation pattern. SYMONS Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa, Canada Received September 9, 1969 Accepted for publication November 12, 1969 At Cobalt the Nipissing diabase intrusive occurs as a 1000 ft (-305 m) thick undulating sheet exposed in a series of basin and arch structures from which 112 specimens were collected at 14 sites. Paleomag- netic analysis of the cleaned natural remanence directions from the 11 acceptable sites suggests that these structures are dominantly primary. Minor post-solidification compression associated with the NW-SE trending faults may have amplified the primary NE-SW axial trends of the structures. Significant folding adjacent to the faults does not appear probable. The origin of the narrow argentiferous veins is probably related to minor local differential movements of large blocks of diabase or to cooling- contraction of the sheet. A revised pole position of 91.9 "E, 19.4 "N (dp = 3.9"; dm = 6.5") is given for the 2140 m.y. old

at 2180 2 40 m.y. by the RbSr whole rock method (Van Schmus 1965) and at 2095 m.y. by the K-A whole rock method (Lowdon et al. 1963). Miller ( 19 10) considered the diabase structure to be primary (i.e. to be formed prior to solidification of the diabase) except for nearly vertical fault offsets. Knight ( 1922) pointed to the gentle dips in the Cobalt Group and concluded that post-solidification folding of the diabase was at most very minor except adjacent to the major NE and NW trending faults. Thomson ( 1957) considered the basin and arch structure to be dominantlv ~rimarv .' The suite is typically tholeitic, and the variety is such as is commonly encountered as a result of differentiation in thick dolerite hills. Some fine grained dolerites are definitely from the Minor Dyke Suite (samples at Site 24 were collected from the younger dykes which cut the main Tumatumari intrusion); others may well be chilled borders from the main Roraima Suite Intrusives. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

ratios found (Hawkes op. cit.), and called for by this crystallization model. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). The cores were oriented in situ with the aid of an astro-compass, (La Rochelle 1961). The three oriented hand samples from Cerro Bolivar were drilled in a press and reoriented in a sand-box. The remanence measurements were made on a spinner magnetometer (Phillips & Kuckes 1967); the alternating-field demagnetization apparatus is described by McElhinny (1963). The Curie Points and saturation magnetization measurements were made on a balance constructed by Collinson (1967). The maximum error, in orientation and measurement, is estimated to be less than 5". Results The palaeomagnetic results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. Preliminary alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization of samples from several sites, in small increments up to 1000 Oe, showed 300 Oe to be the optimum field for routine demagnetization. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. These magnetic properties suggest that the remanence of the upper slate member is composed of two or more components. Probably, the primary d.r.m. or c.r.m. of the upper slates has been mostly obliterated by contact metamorphism during intrusion of the Nipissing sill, which impressed a secondary remanence on the slates. This secondary remanence is probably a t.r.m. associated with heating to a temperature of about 500 f 75 "C, which is the probable Curie Point range for the primary ferromagnetic minerals, or possibly a c.r.m. associated with hydrothermal chemical reactions. Detailed minerdogic studies of the ferromagnetic minerals should distinguish between the t.r.m. and c.r.rn. alterna- tives. It does suggest that a 500 & 75 "C contact metamorphic isotherm could be drawn at or near the base of the upper slate or 20 to 25 ft below the Nipissing sill. Barker (1966) placed a 300 OC isotherm at about the same distance on petrologic evidence. CONCLUSIONS 1. The gabbro is intruded by the Gabcrones granite, and samples from two sites in the granite show almost horizontal magnetization. On initial measurement gabbro samples collected near the contact yield direc- tions close to those of the granite, which suggests that the gabbro was reheated at the time of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). JOURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH VOL. 71, No. 24 D.CEr.R 15, 1966 The Paleomagnetism of the Modipe Gabbro M. E. Ewes  AND M. W. McEIHNNY  Physics Department, University College oJ Rhodesia Salisbury, Rhodesia Samples have been collected from eleven sites in the Modipe gabbro which crops out on the border of Bechuanaland and South Africa. After partial demagnetization in alternating magnetic fields, ten of these sites give almost vertical directions of magnetization, forming a close group which corresponds to a palcomagnetic pole at 33øS, 31øE. The gabbro is intruded by the Gabcrones granite, and samples from two sites in the granite show almost horizontal magnetization. On initial measurement gabbro samples collected near the contact yield direc- tions close to those of the granite, which suggests that the gabbro was reheated at the time of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). After magnetic cleaning, some of these samples give directions which agree with those at the other gabbro sites. Together with detailed alter- nating field and thermal demagnetization studies, this agreement provides strong evidence that the magnetically cleaned directions are those of the TRM acquired when the gabbro originally cooled. at the time of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). After magnetic cleaning, some of these samples give directions which agree with those at the other gabbro sites. Together with detailed alter- nating field and thermal demagnetization studies, this agreement provides strong evidence that the magnetically cleaned directions are those of the TRM acquired when the gabbro originally cooled. The gabbro has an age of approximately 2600 m.y. and is to date the oldest rock unit that has been studied palcomagnetically; the results imply the existence of a geo- magnetic field in this early stage of the earth's history. Alternating field demagnetization ex- periments indicate that some of the magnetic grains have very high coercivities. Thermal demagnetization and IRM studies exclude the presence of hematite and show that the mag- netic mineral present is magnetite. Microscopic observations and theoretical considerations suggest that the high coercivities observed are due to the shape anisotropy of small elongated single-domain grains of magnetite. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. ime possible to classify dikes with any degree of certainty. The study of magnetic properties gives us another tool permitting a definite classification. DIKE SWARMS OF NORTHWEST QUEBEC AND NORTHEAST ONTARIO In the Precambrian Shield of Quebec and Ontario there are several well-developed dike swarms. In parts of the area, in partic- ular the commercially significant greenstone belts, detailed geologic mapping has been done. Recently, wide-scale aeromagnetic surveys have been carried out, showing the presence of a large number of dikes. In the present study a careful compilation of all reported dike exposures and all published airborne magnetic data of a portion of On- tario and Quebec has been made. In the maps accompanying this paper (figs. 1, 2) the compiled data are presented. It can be seen quite clearly that there are several dif- ferent dike swarms with different strike di- rections. The dikes are discussed by Norman (1948), by Moore (1955), by Gill and L'Es- perance (1952) and in the reports of the On- tario Department of Mines, the Quebec Bureau of Mines, and the Geological Survey of Canada. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. SAMPLE COLLECTION AND MEASUREMENT Six hundred and fifty oriented samples were collected from about 350 sites in the initial phase of the program; 225 of these samples are from the six swarms discussed in this report. At each site an attempt was made to collect at least two samples. It would have been desirable to collect more oriented samples at each site, but the additional time required would have meant that the swarms could not have been sampled throughout, a requirement for a concurrent systematic geochemical and petrographic study of the swarms. Two 1-in. cubes were cut from each sample and their magnetization was determined with either a spinner or astatic magnetometer. To eliminate the viscous component of magnetization usually present in igneous rocks, all cubes were subjected to an alternating field whose peak value was empirically set at 80 or 130 oersteds. The reasons for the dispersion within the individual swarms are discussed. e considered unstable. The collec- tion sites of the remaining 53 samples are shown on Fig. 2 and the magnetization directions after washing are plotted in Fig. 10 (a and b). The Matachewan dykes appear to be divisible into two groups whose palaeomagnetic directions are roughly opposed. The magnetization direction of one group is to the northeast (Fig. 10a) and of the other group to the southwest (Fig. lob). This relationship suggests the presence of a pole reversal during the formation of the dyke swarm. Geologically, the Sudbury area is located within the Superior structural province that extends more than 600 miles from the west end of Lake Superior into the province of Quebec. Description of the Irruptive and Associated Rocks Irruptive Rocks The Sudbury irruptive is composed of norite, micropegmatite, and a transi­ tional rock type intermediate between the two. As these rocks have been described in great detail by Walker (1897), Coleman (1903), Phemister (1925 and 1937), Collins ( 1935), and others, only brief petrographic descriptions follow. The transition from norite to micropegmatite is abrupt and has led some geologists, Phemister (1925) in particular, to believe that the irruptive was the result of two separate intrusions. Sudbury Gabbro The Sudbury gabbro forms large sills and dykes in the Huronian and older rocks. Most of it is concentrated in sill-like bodies largely confined to areas of the Bruce Group. Such bodies are numerous in both Copper Cliff and Falcon ­ bridge map-areas, and most of them are several miles long. The gabbro is a dark greenish, equigranular, fairly coarse-grained quartz gabbro, quite different in appearance from the norite of the nickel irruptive. Never­ theless, the quartz gabbro is itself a norite, as was pointed out by Coleman ( 1903) and Barlow ( 1907), for unaltered specimens carry faintly pleochroic hypersthene as well as augite and diallage. The relation of the gabbro to the norite has been described by Cooke ( 1946). The gabbro is older than both the norite and the olivine diabase dykes. Coincidence of Magnetic Vector with Earth's Magnetic Field It is assumed in palaeomagnetic work that the magnetization direction measured in a rock reflects the direction of the earth's magnetic field existing at the time the rocks were magnetized , and that the rocks were magnetized during their formation or soon after. Movement due to flow did not likely disturb the attitude of the vector of magnetization as the Curie point of the magnetic fraction was well below the temperature of solidification of the rocks. They appear to fill simple tension fissures. The olivine diabase is remarkably unaltered, unlike any other basic igneous rocks in the Sudbury district. It consists of "from 60-70 % labradorite, about 20 % augite, half as much olivine and accessory quantities of black iron ore, biotite and apatite" (Kindle, 1933). It is grey on fresh surfaces, but usually weathers reddish brown. The ferromagnetic minerals are mainly ilmenite, highly titaniferous magnetite, and pyrrhotite, in decreasing order of abundance. The magnetic in­ tensity varies from dyke to dyke; dykes of lesser magnetic intensity contain a 2 Introduction greater amount of ilmenite, although the total amount of the ferromagnetic con· stituents remains approximately the same. The magnetic content of the diabase locally affects the compass needle. The dykes cut across all other formations and are definitely later than all folding and faulting within the area. Factors Influencing Remanent Magnetization Other physical and chemical processes may have an effect on remanent magnetization. The magnetic properties of minerals are not completely isotropic, that is, individual grains are not usually magnetized as easily in all directions. This prop­ erty, called magneto-crystalline anisotropy, is related to the crystal lattice. As an example, a crystal of hematite is much more easily magnetized in the C-plane than along the C-axis. The shape of the individual grain also causes anisotropy. However, in an aggregate of minerals, such as is found in norite and olivine dia­ base, where the ferromagnetic constituents are randomly oriented, the net mag­ netization direction is that of the applied field. found to have undergone a relative folding of approximately 30 to 40 degrees after emplacement. The east and northeast parts of the irruptive have been folded as well towards the inside of the basin. The amount of folding is insufficient to support Collins' hypothesis of an originally flat body or Hamilton's hypothesis of an extrusive origin. A modification of Wilson's funnel-shaped intrusion hypothesis appears to fulfil satisfactorily the geological and geophysical requirements. The coordinates for the palaeo-geomagnetic pole positions for the irrup­ tive rocks are found to be appreciably different from those for the olivine diabase dykes. Generalized polar wandering curve for Proterozoic rocks of North America ....... ... ........ .............. ... 20 Vlll PALAEOMAGNETIC STUDY OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE Abstract The palaeomagnetic study of the Sudbury irruptive illustrates the value of palaeomagnetic investigations as an aid in solving certain geological and structural problems. The north and south ranges of the Sudbury irruptive are found to have und

found to have undergone a relative folding of approximately 30 to 40 degrees after emplacement. The east and northeast parts of the irruptive have been folded as well towards the inside of the basin. The amount of folding is insufficient to support Collins' hypothesis of an originally flat body or Hamilton's hypothesis of an extrusive origin. A modification of Wilson's funnel-shaped intrusion hypothesis appears to fulfil satisfactorily the geological and geophysical requirements. The coordinates for the palaeo-geomagnetic pole positions for the irrup­ tive rocks are found to be appreciably different from those for the olivine diabase dykes. In some places where the diabase intrudes the norite, the resultant direction of magnetization conforms locally with that of the dykes. Correlation with pole positions from other North American Precambrian rocks indicates that a considerable time interval separated their respective times of intrusion, the diabase dykes being the younger. Ar/ Ar analyses of biotite and feldspars from neighboring schists also indicate the presence of two mild thermal events, at 1.5 Ga and 0.6 Ga. Paleomagnetic analyses of samples from these same metamorphic rocks reveal three components of magnetization. The predominant and most stable component (273°E, 21°N) is considered to have been acquired as a result of post Eburnean upfift and coofing at ~2.0 Ga, whereas the two less stable components with poles at 2350E, 430N and 16*E, 36"N, probably correlate with the 1.5 Ga and 0.6 Ga thermal pulses, respectively. Rock units from southern Liberia also yield two secondary magnetizations, one at 247~E, 370N and the other at 104*E, o 40 39 5 N, and a 1.5 Ga Ar/ Ar date on plagioclase. (1984) demonstrated the agreement between contemporaneous 1.95 Ga paleomagnetic poles from the West African Shield in southern Liberia and the Guiana Shield in Venezuela when the Atlantic was closed. Introduction The Jatulian sequence of sedimentary rocks forms the basal cover on the approximately 2 700 m.y. old Precambrian gneissous basement complex in eastern Finland and Karelia. The group typically starts with Sariola (Eskola 1925) conglomerate overlain by a thick series of quartzites. These are followed by dolomites and pelitic schists (the so-called Marine Jatuli, Väy- rynen 1928). The Jatulian rocks are frequently accompanied by dikes, sills and effusive beds of subsilicic composition (Väyrynen 1928, Piirainen 1969, Silvennoinen 1972). Some of then are tholeitic but the majority are spilitic. According to Sakko (1971), zircon and sphene yield a radio- metric age of 2 150 m.y. for these magmatic rocks. The Jatulian sequence is well exposed in easter

uently accompanied by dikes, sills and effusive beds of subsilicic composition (Väyrynen 1928, Piirainen 1969, Silvennoinen 1972). Some of then are tholeitic but the majority are spilitic. According to Sakko (1971), zircon and sphene yield a radio- metric age of 2 150 m.y. for these magmatic rocks. The Jatulian sequence is well exposed in eastern Finland where a narrow band rich in quartzites starting from north of Lake Ladoga in the south runs to Lapland in the north. The sedimentary rocks of the group are usually devoid of magnetic minerals, and consequently, the magnetic survey of the sequence has to be made on the intrusive dikes and effusive layers. To find out whether these rocks were suitable for this type of work, samples were collected from four different areas in eastern Finland. A total of 32 locations were sampled and tested for magnetic stability. INTRODUCTION Palaeomagnetic data of Precambrian rocks can be used to analyze whether pre-Mesozoic horizontal motions have taken place within or between dif- ferent shields. Relative movements between lithospheric units are indicated by differences in the APW paths of the units. If the different provinces of a shield show different APW paths, the plate tectonic model can be used to describe the evolution of the shield (Piper et al., 1973; Cavanaugh and Seyfert, 1977). However, if the APW curves are similar, the ensialic within- shield tectonics is the proper model (McElhinny and McWilliams, 1977). Dissimilar APW curves of different shields indicate that the shields have drifted independently and emphasize that the opening and closing of oceans is a recurrent feature in the earth’s history (b’ilson, 1966; Spall, 1973). In order to find out whether relative motions of lithospheric units have 624 taken place, accurate APW paths are needed for each shield. In this paper we present a new APW path for the Baltic Shield which supersedes the simpler paths previously proposed (e.g. Neuvonen, 1970; Spall, 1973; Poorter, 1975). Errors in sampling and measurement, insufficiently eliminated secular variation and discrepancies between radiometric and magnetization ages can cause considerable scatter of palaeopoles (see also Irving and McGlynn, this volume, Chapter 23, and McWilliams, this volume, Chapter 26, ed.). Secondary components The Precambrian rocks of the Baltic Shield have been affected by several metamorphic events (e.g. KOUVO, 1976; Merilainen, 1976; Gad et al., 1978), each of which has added another component to the magnetic and radio- metric record carried by the rocks. Some of the investigated ultrabasics probably belong to the tholeiitic, and some to the komatiitic rock series, and the characteristics are presented in this report. Paleomagnetic measurements were tested for classification in 9 different types of ultrabasic bodies. On the basis of the sampling and analysis of till, the geochemistry and heavy-mineral composition of the till cover above a hidden ultramafic body can be concluded to (reflect) the characteristic features of the ultramafic rock type. The opaque minerals were mainly oxides, chromite and magnetite; nickel sulfides, pentlandite, millerite and heazlewoodite were also common. Some bodies, especially those containing mag- nesite, were characterized by accessory nickel arsenides. Two areas were rec- ommended for future prospecting operations. Summary: The ultramafics of Lapland. Geologinen tutkimus- laitos, Tutkimusraportti N:o 23. 87 pages, 32 figures and 9 tables. During 1974 - 1976 an investigation of the ultrabasic rocks of Lapland was performed by the Institute of Geology and Mineralogy, University of Turku, in co- operation with Outokumpu Oy and the Geochemical Department of the Geological Survey in Finland. The research was supported by the Ministry of Trade and Indus- try. A total of about 3500 samples was collected from the mapped 171 ultrabasic or basic bodies in different parts of Lapland. They were classified on the basis of geological field data as well as on petrological and geochemical criteria. The com- prehensive analytical and field data is presented in a separate data report, which is stored in the Geological Survey of Finland. Some of the investigated ultrabasics probably belong to the tholeiitic, and some to the komatiitic rock series, and the characteristics are presented in this report. As shown in figure 1, the Matachewan dikes are a swarm with a north-south strike. These are probably the oldest dikes, as they can be seen to be cut off by the younger flat-lying Precambrian rocks exposed in the portions of the shield near the Grenville Front. These younger flat-lying rocks are the Cobalt sedi- ments and the Nipissing diabase sill. The age of these flat-lying rocks is not yet fully agreed upon, but they are generally consid- ered to be about 1.5 billion years. Where the dikes have been carefully mapped, as for example in the Timmins area (Hogg, 1954), it is clear that there are man

An average inclination of - 100 falls within the circle of confidence of all the Matachewan north-south dikes. The use of the direction of remanent magnetism has thus enabled us to distinguish very definitely between the various dike swarms. In figure 4 a plot of declination versus in- clination is presented. In this figure the re- sults of Precambrian remanent-magnetism studies from the Lake Superior-Ontario- Quebec area are presented. It can readily be seen that a fairly smooth curve can be drawn through all the points. is presented. In Scotland the relative ages of the dikes could be determined with some accuracy by the strata they intruded. In the Canadian Shield area, with one exception, there are no overlying strata to permit classification, so it is necessary to resort to other, less ob- vious criteria for classification. The most useful of these is the strike of the dike in relation to that of other dikes, but this is not always adequate, as swarms of different ages may have the same strikes. Anderson (1951) has made a thorough study of the dikes of Scotland and the mechanics of their intrusion. He points out that dikes tend to have a fairly constant width and to be equally spaced. This means that width and separation may also be useful criteria for dike classification. One other method of classification has been a careful study of composition, a cri- terion useful in only a few particular cases. The usual classification is one where we have olivine diabase, quartz diabase, or simple diabase. In the process of crystallization of diabasic magma it has been found that oli- vine and quartz are mutually exclusive, and it is supposed that the dikes of various com- positions are formed from different magmas. Unfortunately quartz and olivine are only present in small q

ime possible to classify dikes with any degree of certainty. The study of magnetic properties gives us another tool permitting a definite classification. DIKE SWARMS OF NORTHWEST QUEBEC AND NORTHEAST ONTARIO In the Precambrian Shield of Quebec and Ontario there are several well-developed dike swarms. In parts of the area, in partic- ular the commercially significant greenstone belts, detailed geologic mapping has been done. Recently, wide-scale aeromagnetic surveys have been carried out, showing the presence of a large number of dikes. In the present study a careful compilation of all reported dike exposures and all published airborne magnetic data of a portion of On- tario and Quebec has been made. In the maps accompanying this paper (figs. 1, 2) the compiled data are presented. It can be seen quite clearly that there are several dif- ferent dike swarms with different strike di- rections. Evans and Bingham (19731, incor- porating their paleomagnetic data with the published radiometric ages, suggested an age of 1730 + 1830 Ma for the Martin Formation. They also established that the hematitization preceded the folding, and thus must have taken place almost immediately after deposition. Paleocurrent measurements (Tremblay, 1972, Fig. 5) show that sediments in the Martin Lake Basin were derived from both sides of the basin and suggest that the basin was initially not significantly larger than at present. The locally- derived basal conglomerates reinforce that conclusion (Fraser et al., 1970). The depositional environments of the Martin Formation redbeds range from talus slopes, alluvial fans and braided streams to lacustrine. RESULTS OF THE MEASUREMENTS The direction and intensity of the remanent magnetiza- tion of the specimens from the volcanics were measured with an astatic magnetometer and those of the sediment samples with a spinner magnetometer with higher sensitivity. Alternating field and thermal demagnetization was performed in up to 27 steps on at least two specimens per site in order to evaluate in detail coercivity and blocking temperature ranges. If the direction remained constant in all test specimens and showed good coherency the rest of the specimens of the same site were treated at a single tempera- ture or field strength. In all other cases, the rest of the specimens of the site were treated in a range of field strengths (up to 60 mT) or heated to a series of increasing temperatures and the remanence remeasured after each step. Iron Formation Lithofacies Laminated Iron Formation This is the predominant form of iron formation in Sayunei Formation. It is characterized by alternating laminae of hematite and jasper. Either component may dominate to form jasper-rich or hematite-rich bands and/or lenticular patches up to several centimetres thick. Contacts between the bands are generally sharp and even, coincident with lamination, but contacts between patchy areas are typically diffuse and irregular. Laminae may be traced continuously across their lateral contacts. Irregular hematite-rich patches within jasper-rich areas suggest local diagenetic iron enrichment. ins. The lowest unit, the Mount Berg Formation, is a grey-green mixtite seen only in the southern Mackenzie Mountains. Conformably above this, the Sayunei Formation is dominated by maroon to red, silty rhythmites with abundant dropstones. Conformably overlying this, the Shezal Formation successively comprises maroon and greenish grey mixtites. These two formations outcrop discontinuously throughout the southern and central Mackenzie Mountains. A homologous succession of rhythmites and mixtites is present in the Upper Tindir Group in Alaska. In the northern Mackenzie Mountains, however, only red and greenish grey mixtites occur. Jasper-hematite iron formation of probable rift-related, volcanogenic hydrothermal origin was found in the red mixtites of the northern Mackenzies as well as in the upper Sayunei and Tindir rhythmites. The Rapitan Group lies not far below the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary and overlies rocks judged to be about 0.8 Ga old. Except locally, the basal contact is distinctly unconformable. This unconf ormity marks the last major faulting event before the Paleozoic Era. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: G.M. Yeo The Rapitan Group (sensu stricto) includes maroon and grey rnixtites, silty rhythmites, conglomerates, sandstones, and iron formation (Fig. 2.2). Maroon rhythmites of the Sayunei Formation are the basal unit over most of the Mountain River and Redstone River areas. In Thundercloud Range, however, mixtites underlie the Sayunei. Maroon rnixtites of the Snake River Tillite member of the Shezal Formation take the place of the Sayunei rhythmites in Snake River area. Maroon rnixtites of the Shezal Formation also locally overlie the Sayunei Formation. The upper Shezal Formation comprises mainly greenish grey mixtites. Jasper- hematite iron formation occurs in both the Shezal and Sayunei formations. Overyling the Rapitan Group are recessive, friable to fissile, dark grey shale and minor sandstone of the Twitya Formation. The Twitya interfingers with and is overlain by characteristically resistant carbonates, sandstones, and silt- stones of the Keele Formation. The Proterozoic succession is capped by recessive mudstones of the Sheepbed Formation. To emphasize their distinctness from the underlying clastics these three units have been collectively called the Hay Creek Group (Yeo, 1978; Young et al., 1979). This paper is concerned with tholeiitic basalts of the Kinojevis Group (Jensen 19784, 1979, 1981). We studied the AN ET AL. 437 paleomagnetism of four geologically and petrologically well characterized "sites" in Kinojevis flows in order to determine in detail the nature of their NRM. Detailed mapping indicates that flows at all of these areas were deposited horizontally and deformed only by simple tilting. A "primary" remanence, if indeed one exists, should be corrected for regional structure. General geology I The area sampled (Fig. 1) is part of Goodwin and Ridler's (1970) Noranda-Benoit volcanic complex, in the central Abitibi Belt. As this paper represents our initial studies of the paleomagnetism of this belt, the geology of the area is described in relative detail here; in other papers only the most pertinent aspects are included. The Ontario portion of the complex is composed of three subalkalic volcanic cycles, each associated with sedimentation and intrusion of comagmatic units (Jensen 1978a, 1981). The paleomagnetic data from Kinojevis tholeiites indicate the emplacement, burial, and tight downwarping of the 10 km or so of Kinojevis stratigraphy were nearly synchronous with Matachewan intrusion. GEOLOGICAL FEATURES All of the four iron formation deposits are Archean BIF of the magnetite oxide facies with three located in the Abitibi Belt and one in the Uchi Belt of the Superior Province in the Canadian Shield. GEOLOGICAL FEATURES All of the four iron formation deposits are Archean BIF of the magnetite oxide facies with three located in the Abitibi Belt and one in the Uchi Belt of the Superior Province in the Canadian Shield. The BIF horizons range in thickness from -50 to -150 m and are interlayered with siliceous metasediments associated with Archean metavolcanics of basic to acidic composition. These strata were deformed during the Kenoran Orogeny at -2.55 Ga at which time minor basic and large acidic plutons were emplaced adjacent to or within a few kilometers of the deposits. Natural Remanent Magnetization The NAF for the NRM of the four deposits is 0.19. or 19%. Given the large variety of attitudes of the BIF in these deposits, the NAF represents a reasonable value regardless of the attitude of a given BIF. The NAF represents the swing of viscous remanence components (VRM) into alignment with the EMF, and thus has the effect of increasing the induced magnetization regardless of the attitude of the BIF. The presence of significant VRM components is well documented from alternating field (AF) demagnetization, thermal (Th) demagnetization, and VRM decay tests such as storage and shock tests. The hard remanence components cannot be calculated in general terms unless the specific orientation of their vectors and their magnitudes are known. The mean natural remanent magnetization (NRM) 2 5 -3 intensities for the IF and HR are 2.1 x 10 and 1.47 x 10 emu cm which give mean Koenigsberger ratios of 0.66 and 0.051 respectively. Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. GEOLOGICAL FEATURES All of the four iron formation deposits are Archean BIF of the magnetite oxide facies with three located in the Abitibi Belt and one in the Uchi Belt of the Superior Province in the Canadian Shield. The BIF horizons range in thickness from -50 to -150 m and are interlayered with siliceous metasediments associated with Archean metavolcanics of basic to acidic composition. These strata were deformed during the Kenoran Orogeny at -2.55 Ga at which time minor basic and large acidic plutons were emplaced adjacent to or within a few kilometers of the deposits. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. The BIF horizons range in thickness from -50 to -150 m and are interlayered with siliceous metasediments associated with Archean metavolcanics of basic to acidic composition. These strata were deformed during the Kenoran Orogeny at -2.55 Ga at which time minor basic and large acidic plutons were emplaced adjacent to or within a few kilometers of the deposits. Natural Remanent Magnetization The NAF for the NRM of the four deposits is 0.19. or 19%. Given the large variety of attitudes of the BIF in these deposits, the NAF represents a reasonable value regardless of the attitude of a given BIF. The NAF represents the swing of viscous remanence components (VRM) into alignment with the EMF, and thus has the effect of increasing the induced magnetization regardless of the attitude of the BIF. The presence of significant VRM components is well documented from alternating field (AF) demagnetization, thermal (Th) demagnetization, and VRM decay tests such as storage and shock tests. The hard remanence components cannot be calculated in general terms unless the specific orientation of their vectors and their magnitudes are known. The mean natural remanent magnetization (NRM) 2 5 -3 intensities for the IF and HR are 2.1 x 10 and 1.47 x 10 emu cm which give mean Koenigsberger ratios of 0.66 and 0.051 respectively. Thus the HR contribution to the residual anomaly may be neglected. The NRM for the IF augments the calculated anomaly intensity by 14%. Combining the AMS and NRM augmenting effects with a demagnetizing factor of 2 77, yields theoretical anomaly calculations for the North and South Pit deposits that are within 10% of the measured anomalies in terms of peak intensity and half -width. Utilizing alternating field, thermal and chemical demagnetization techniques along with fold and contact tests for remanence stability leads to the isolation of three Archean remanence components in both the IF and HR. The GM2 component is the oldest at ^2.8Ga and records primary deposition or diagenesis. It may also reflect tectonic motions between the Uchi and Abitibi Belts. The GM1 component is most prevalent and records a predeformational metamorphic event at ~2.75 Ga. Its agreement with the primary components isolated in the 20 Archean strata of the Abitibi Felt may indicate a genetic link between the two events. INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetism can be used to determine the genesis of some iron ore deposits by comparing the remanence direction of the ore deposit with that of the host rock or of other rocks of known age from the same geologic pro- vince, and by determining whether the remanence of the ore deposit was acquired before or after folding. Thus a syngenetic deposit has a prefolding remanence which it acquired during the time interval between deposition of the enclosing rock formations. By this method, Gross and Strangway (1961) concluded that the "deep hard hematite" deposit at F'Derik in Mauritania is a Precambrian syngenetic deposit and that the "surficial hard hematite" deposit at Rouessa West is a Cenozoic laterite. Similarly, DuBois (1961, 1962) demonstrated that a hard hematite deposit in Cumberland, England, is an epigenetic deposit of Permian-Triassic age in host rocks of Lower Carboni- ferous age. INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetism can be used to determine the genesis of some iron ore deposits by comparing the remanence direction of the ore deposit with that of the host rock or of other rocks of known age from the same geologic pro- vince, and by determining whether the remanence of the ore deposit was acquired before or after folding. Thus a syngenetic deposit has a prefolding remanence which it acquired during the time interval between deposition of the enclosing rock formations. By this method, Gross and Strangway (1961) concluded that the "deep hard hematite" deposit at F'Derik in Mauritania is a Precambrian syngenetic deposit and that the "surficial hard hematite" deposit at Rouessa West is a Cenozoic laterite. etrography were given by Shaw (1985). Matachewan dykes are by far the most numerous. Lithologically, they are quartz diabases, often con- taining the diagnostic green plagioclase phenocrysts. In gen- eral, they are moderately to heavily altered (50-80%), with groundmass plagioclase replaced by sausserite and chlorite, and pyroxene extensively uralitized, especially around the margins. Despite alteration, however, the lath shape and twin- ing of plagioclase are still visible in most dykes. Two dykes, at sites 2 and 4, were remarkably fresh and exhibited higher natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities and more stable, higher coercivity characteristic components that gave well-defined site directions (Appendix). In the altered dykes, only about 10% of NRM intensity remained after 20 mT demagnetization, with further demagnetization required to yield a stable end point. Compared with the fresh dykes, how- ever, stable end points were defined with lower precision (mean angular deviation was 5 10" compared with 55"). These dykes have been documented, mainly through paleomagnetic studies, in the Abitibi Belt (e.g., Strangway 1964; Pesonen 1973; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Condie et al. 1987) and also in a region extending from Hearst to Wawa on the western side of the KSZ (Ernst and Halls 1984). Matache- wan dykes are recognized in the field by the presence of pale green feldspar phenocrysts and in the laboratory by a dual magnetic polarity (declination: D = 30"/210° ; inclination: I = +lo0/-10"). Their paleomagnetic signature is unique amongst Canadian Shield dykes and serves to distinguish them, especially where they lack phenocrysts, from dykes of younger swarms. Although many of the dykes shown in Fig. 2 are likely to be Matachewan, others of similar trend, but belonging to three younger groups, may be present. North of the Huronian fold belt (HFB in Fig. 1) in the Elliot Lake area, Aibangbee (1982) mapped northwest-trending quartz diabase dykes that both predate and postdate the basal Huronian sedimentary units. etrography were given by Shaw (1985). Matachewan dykes are by far the most numerous. Lithologically, they are quartz diabases, often con- taining the diagnostic green plagioclase phenocrysts. In gen- eral, they are moderately to heavily altered (50-80%), with groundmass plagioclase replaced by sausserite and chlorite, and pyroxene extensively uralitized, especially around the margins. Despite alteration, however, the lath shape and twin- ing of plagioclase are still visible in most dykes. Two dykes, at sites 2 and 4, were remarkably fresh and exhibited higher natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities and more stable, higher coercivity characteristic components that gave well-defined site directions (Appendix). In the altered dykes, only about 10% of NRM intensity remained after 20 mT demagnetization, with further demagnetization required to yield a stable end point. Compared with the fresh dykes, how- ever, stable end points were defined with lower precision (mean angular deviation was 5 10" compared with 55"). Many altered dykes, lithologically indistinguishable from Matachewan types, particularly those along the Montreal River, did not contain any coherent magnetization (Appendix), whereas others yielded poorly determined directions based on only one or tw

directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: Matachewan swarm, trends north to northwest and is composed of quartz tholeiite dykes that are found in virtually every part of a 500 km wide swath of Archean shield that borders Lake Superior to the east and northeast. These dykes have been documented, mainly through paleomagnetic studies, in the Abitibi Belt (e.g., Strangway 1964; Pesonen 1973; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Condie et al. 1987) and also in a region extending from Hearst to Wawa on the western side of the KSZ (Ernst and Halls 1984). Matache- wan dykes are recognized in the field by the presence of pale green feldspar phenocrysts and in the laboratory by a dual magnetic polarity (declination: D = 30"/210° ; inclination: I = +lo0/-10"). Their paleomagnetic signature is unique amongst Canadian Shield dykes and serves to distinguish them, especially where they lack phenocrysts, from dykes of younger swarms. Although many of the dykes shown in Fig. 2 are likely to be Matachewan, others of similar trend, but belonging to three younger groups, may be present. North of the Huronian fold belt (HFB in Fig. 1) in the Elliot Lake area, Aibangbee (1982) mapped northwest-trending quartz diabase dykes that both predate and postdate the basal Huronian sedimentary units. Nipissing diabase intrusions consist mainly of pyroxene gabbro and hornblende gabbro, but differentiation has led to the formation of minor amounts of feldspathic pyroxenite, gabbroic anorthosite, and granophyre. Olivine is present in several intrusions in the Cobalt and Englehart areas but the typical mafic minerals are augite, hypersthene, hornblende, and minor biotite. Calcic plagioclase, quartz, sulphides, iron - titanium oxides (ilmenite - titaniferous magnetite and ilmenite -hematite), and minor apatite form the remainder. Major- and minor-element chemistry indicates that all of these rocks formed from magma of similar composition with differ- entiation mainly by gravitative settling of early-formed mafic minerals with consequent depletion of residual liquids in Mg and Ca and enrichment in iron and alkalis. Major- and minor-element chemistry indicates that all of these rocks formed from magma of similar composition with differ- entiation mainly by gravitative settling of early-formed mafic minerals with consequent depletion of residual liquids in Mg and Ca and enrichment in iron and alkalis. Alteration of the Nipissing Diabase, whether by low-grade regional metamorphism as in the Sudbury area (Card 1978) or by deuteric alteration as in the Cobalt area, resulted in replace- ment of the primary minerals by uralitic amphiboles, albite, epidote, chlorite, and quartz or quartz -feldspar intergrowths. The primary ilmenite - magnetite and ilmenite - hematite intergrowths are replaced by magnetite - sphene - leucoxene aggregates. In addition, uralitization of the mafic minerals commonly results in formation of fine-grained oxides and sul- phides. Also cutting the Huronian rocks are northeast-trending quartz diabase dykes of the Preissac swarm with an 40Ar- 39Ar isotopic age of 2150 Ma (Hanes and York 1979) and younger northeast trending olivine diabase dykes of the Abitibi swarm with a U-Pb baddeleyite age of 1140 Ma (Krogh et al. 1987). This involved stepwise AF demagnetiza- tion to eliminate the softer components before the stepwise thermal cleaning was begun. PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). The unaltered host rocks have a stable pre-folding remanence of probable Keewatin age, whereas the ore and adjacent altered host rocks have a stable post-folding remanence of possibly Early to Middle Keweenawan age. This result indicates that the ore originated as a post-folding epigenetic deposit. INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetism is useful in studying the genesis of hard hematite ore deposits. The genesis of the hard hematite ore deposits at Ely and Soudan on the Vermilion Range, Minnesota, U.S.A. (Fig. 1) has been disputed. Winchell and Winchell (1891) proposed that they are anamorphosed primary chemical sediments. Clements (1903) and Abbott (1907) proposed that iron-bearing groundwater solutions metasomatically replaced the primary iron-formation in structural troughs. Van Hise and Leith (1911) argued that groundwater leached and oxidized the primary iron-formation to form residual soft hematite deposits, which at Soudan were metamorphosed directly to hard hematite and at Ely were weathered to laterites and then metamorphosed. DISCUSSION Magnetic Overprints Polyphase magnetization is the rule rather than the exception in these early Proterozoic formations. Detailed demagnetization studies are sometimes effective in isolating the various magnetic components but it is quite probable that many apparently aberrant data are caused by unresolved composite magnetizations. One effective way of investigating polyphase remanence is to consider the magnetic vectors removed during each step in incremental demagnetization runs. In bedded sequences whose magnetization is entirely secondary, the present hori- zontal usually is assumed to approximate the paleomagnetic horizontal because the dispersion of paleodirections is mark- edly better before than after correction for bedding attitudes. This simple-eitherlor-rationale, while still applicable to rock units with uncom~licated histories. is now known to be inapplicable in many instances because magnetization pro- cesses can occur over an interval of time that extends from before to after deformation. As the list of rock units with fairly simple thermal and chemical histories is exhausted, and those with more complex histories come to be studied, paleomag- netists will encounter more and more frequently such extended magnetization processes, and will have to face the concomitant problem of determining the paleomagnetic horizontal. One of the hallmarks of rock units with such extended mag- netization histories is that the dispersion of paleodirections is high both before and after correction for bedding-higher, that is, than can be reasonably anticipated from paleosecular varia- tion. The dacites we have assigned to the Marama Formation of Church (1973) are the youngest rocks sampled. Two sites are reversely magnetized (38, 39) and three (7, 13, and 15) are normal. Church (1980b) observed normal polarity at one site in Marama dacite. Therefore, at least two reversals occurred, one above and one within the base of the Marron Formation, confining it, in all probability, to one normal polarity chron. C., Canada V8L 4B2 Received June 7, 1988 Revision accepted November 22, 1988 The middle Eocene Marron volcanics (mean age 52 f 2 Ma) of the Kelowna outlier form the upper part of the hanging wall of the westerly dipping Okanagan Valley fault (OVF) in south-central British Columbia. They overlie Quesnellia. The OVF is currently interpreted as the westernmost member of a network of low-angle extension faults in the southern Omenica belt. The OVF was active in the middle Eocene at much the same time that the Marron volcanics were cooling. Relative to present horizontal, the magnetizations are widely scattered (Fisher's precision parameter k = 8) and after correction for bedding attitudes, there is no significant improvement (k = 9). Evidently, some magnetizations were acquired before (referred to as category 1) and others after (category 2) tilting; that is, the horizontal plane at the time of magnetization some- times did and sometimes did not coincide with the bedding plane.
